t: the gifts were not accepted, yet the leper became fit. Even though the gifts were not accepted, the leper became fit to eat of the sacred offerings. The later authorities disagree about the significance of the gifts not having been accepted (see Even HaAzel on this halakhah, Minchat Chinukh 176:2, Arukh HaShulchan 237:6).
a leper who was afflicted after he brought his guilt offering. Even if he had not yet had time to bring his other offerings.
he needs another offering for the second leprosy. Since from the time he brought his guilt offering he left the status of the first leprosy, he does not fulfill his obligation with a single offering.
and he brought his birds. Together with the other items he brings for his purification after being healed of leprosy (above 4:1).

one offering for all of them. Even though he was healed in the interim, since he had not yet managed to bring his guilt offering, it is considered one long leprosy, and therefore he fulfills his obligation with one offering (Rashi, Keritot 9b).

a poor person's offering. A poor leper brings a lamb for a guilt offering and two birds, one as a sin offering and one as a burnt offering, in place of the three sheep the rich person brings (above 1:3).

and afterwards one of the lepers died. And now the blood of the second sin offering cannot be sprinkled, lest it belong to the leper who died, and a sin offering whose owner died is left to die and is not offered on the altar (Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 4:1).
perhaps the one whose blood was sprinkled was his sin offering. And since his sin offering was already offered, he cannot bring another sin offering.
and one does not bring a sin offering of an animal on account of doubt. Ibid. 7:10.

for a rich person who brought a poor person's offering has not fulfilled his obligation. And since the bird sin offering is a poor person's offering, a rich person cannot bring it even as a doubtful offering (see ibid.).
let him write all his property to another and be found poor. Let him write a deed of gift of all his property to another person, and thereby become poor.
for the vower's means suffice. For the one who vowed is wealthy.

for this vower is obligated to bring the offerings of a rich person. And he does not fulfill his obligation with a poor person's offering (above 5:10; see also Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 14:9 and the commentary there).
